title: Localized Decoherence as a Constructive Tool: An Optical Simulation of Matter-Wave Interference
authors: Hadis Torbatiyan, Bedir Halcı, Adrian Udovičić, Lara Ulčakar, Rainer Kaltenbaek
abstract: Decoherence is conventionally regarded as a detrimental process that suppresses quantum coherence and limits the performance of quantum technologies. Contrary to this view, we show that spatially localized decoherence can instead be exploited as an interferometric tool. Beyond its conceptual implications, localized decoherence provides a novel approach to prepare arbitrary macroscopic spatial superpositions for testing quantum physics with massive particles. We demonstrate the proof of principle by making use of the correspondence between optics and matter-waves through the equivalence of the respective propagation functions. By employing stochastic phase fields to the optical counterpart to model the decoherence, our experiments confirm the expected interference. The results establish localized decoherence as a resource for quantum state engineering.
summary: This research demonstrates that localized decoherence is not merely a source of noise but can be harnessed as a functional resource in quantum interferometry. By simulating matter-wave interference using optical beams modulated by random phase patterns, the authors confirm that specific decoherence profiles yield predictable and controllable interference patterns. This establishes a new paradigm for quantum state engineering using controlled decoherence.
main_problem: The paper explores the counter-intuitive idea that spatially localized decoherence, usually seen as detrimental, can be actively exploited as a constructive tool for matter-wave interferometry.
main_result: The simulations and experiments confirm that localized decoherence can generate measurable interference patterns, providing a novel resource for engineering arbitrary spatial superpositions of massive particles.
method: The study uses an optical simulation approach, mapping the physics of matter-wave interference onto the paraxial propagation of classical optical beams modulated by a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM).
model_or_system: The system involves matter-wave interferometry simulated optically, comparing theoretical predictions for different decoherence profiles: Opaque Disk (OD), Gaussian Opacity (GO), and Periodic Opacity (PO).
key_observables: Interference intensity patterns (e.g., Arago spot, Talbot carpets), central intensity at the beam axis, and the visibility of interference fringes.
important_parameters: Decoherence parameters ($\sigma$, $a$), propagation distance ($z$), and experimental parameters like SLM efficiency ($\eta$) and phase deviation ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is the validity of the correspondence between matter-wave evolution and optical beam propagation, though discrepancies in fitting suggest limitations in the model equations used.
figures_summary: Figures compare experimental measurements of interference patterns (OD, GO, PO) against theoretical predictions, often including fits that account for experimental imperfections like SLM efficiency.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical framework linking decoherence to interference, through detailed modeling of various decoherence geometries (OD, GO, PO), and culminates in comparing these models against quantitative experimental data and fitting observed deviations.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum foundations (decoherence) with experimental quantum optics, providing a concrete, controllable method to generate and test complex quantum states using optical tools.
